newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's Kia Motors plans new Asian car.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kia Motors plans new Asian car.

text.p: South Korea's Kia Motors announced on Tuesday it would build a string of parts and assembly plants from China to Indonesia to produce a new Asian car.
The country's number two carmaker, fleeing a saturated domestic market, said it aimed to assemble 300,000 compact cars in Asia annually by 2001, drawing on parts from far-flung production centres.
Parts factories would be located in seven Asian nations, also including Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, India and Iran, a company official said.
They would feed into a knockdown kit assembly network throughout Asia. Indonesia would be the main assembly centre with annual capacity of 120,000 units, the official said.
"The model will be an upgrade of the Sephia compact car or the Pride. Its engine capacity will be less than 1.5 litres," the official said.
He gave no details of the value of the investment.
Kia said on Monday its annual overseas production would increase to 520,000 units by 2001 from 69,042 in 1996 and total overseas sales would expand to 800,000 units from 321,950.
By 2001 Kia plans to make vehicles in 16 countries, including Egypt, Brazil, Russia and Poland.
Kia currently exports Sephia cars assembled in South Korea to Indonesia under the model name Timor as part of Indonesia's national car project.
Other South Korean carmakers, including Daewoo Motor, a unit of the Daewoo Group, are also scrambling to find new production bases and markets offshore.

Analysts said South Korea's car industry may see lower sales this year for the first time in many years. Exports have been battered by a weaker yen, which has made Japanese cars more competitive, and slumping consumer confidence at home.
"The business climate looks pretty bad this year," said Lee Kyu-young, an analyst at the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association. "We may have to expect negative growth."
The association last year forecast a modest 7.8 percent rise in vehicle sales in 1997 after 14 percent growth in 1995.
But a month of wildcat strikes in January hit the auto industry hardest, adding to woes created by a slowing economy. Profit margins at leading automakers, including Kia, are now wafer thin.
South Korean car exports jumped 23.7 percent to 1.21 milion units in 1996, thanks mainly to a drive by automakers to expand overseas markets and improve quality, the association said.
But analysts predicted overseas sales growth would slow to less than 10 percent this year.
"The domestic market is close to saturation as demand from first-time car buyers is almost filled up," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
"Competition will be cut-throat in the domestic market," said Kim Ahn-kang, an analyst at the research arm of Hyundai Motor Co, the country's largest carmaker.
